title: B-R-A
hookLine: bara: to create, in the Torah used only of God

cards: The Torah's opening line has a subject and a verb. The subject is God. The verb is bara.
Bereshit bara Elohim: in the beginning, God created. English is generous with create. People create playlists, problems, a stir at the dinner table.
Hebrew has plenty of words for making and building, and people use them all the time. But this one, in the Torah, is kept for a single subject. Bet, resh, alef: B-R-A.
A verb with a reserved seat.

teach.b: You met that opening line on day twenty-two. Now, its verb. Turn it four ways.
First, the subject. Jewish commentators point out that in the Torah, bara is used only of God. People make, build, shape and plant.
God creates. Second, the surprises. Bara turns up at the start, "God created the heaven and the earth," then goes quiet.
When it returns, it's for something unexpected: "And God created the great sea-monsters." Not the sun or the trees, but the creatures of the deep.
Some readers take that as a hint that even the things people fear most are inside creation, not outside it. Then it comes three times in one verse, for human beings.
Third, the pair. On the seventh day, God rests from all His work "which God in creating had made," in the old Jewish Publication Society translation. Creating, bara.
Made, asah. Some Jewish commentators read the Hebrew as created to make, and hear an unfinished world: God creates, and leaves the making to go on in human hands. Fourth, the heart.

teach.h: THE HEART: CREATE ME A CLEAN HEART.
teach.b: A psalm asks for this verb to happen again, inside a person: "Create me a clean heart, O God."
Not fix, not repair. Create, as if some things need more than patching. So the verb at the top of the Torah returns in a prayer, as a request for something new.

how: Jews begin the yearly cycle of Torah reading with Bereshit, "in the beginning," and Jewish commentators often note that the verb bara, to create, is reserved in the Torah for God.

o: a root for blessing, as in a blessing over bread
a root for creating, a verb the Torah keeps for God
a root for building, as with bricks or a house

s: in the Torah, people bara things all the time
commentators point out that in the Torah, bara is used only of God. people make, build and shape.
in Genesis 1, bara returns for the great sea-monsters
the seventh-day verse uses only one verb for creation
it pairs two: "which God in creating had made": created, and made.

games.q: the creation story is ending, and the text needs a verb for what God rested from. which does it use?
o: both: "which God in creating had made."
games.why: both verbs, side by side. some commentators hear in it a world left with making still to do.

practice: Make one small thing that wasn't here a minute ago, nothing useful and nothing anyone will grade: a line of words, a doodle in a margin, a few notes hummed in a new order, a paper fold.
Don't fix it or judge it; just notice what it's like to bring one new thing into the room. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's line about a clean heart while you work.

wordCard.voice: B-R-A. Bet, resh, alef: the root of bara, to create, the verb of the Torah's opening line, which in the Torah has God as its subject. Today's word.
